Dukh-sam-yog-vi-yog-

That in which there is no conjunction of sorrows

Shrimad Bhagavad Gita:

Vid-yat-
= to know
Abhyas
[ Chapter 6
Anir-vi-ñña-chetasa = not being deluded
Having been
Sam-yog-kā hi sā = that very conjunction is
Vi-yog = separation,
= that very conjunction (which is the goal of
Dhyana-yog-kā = meditation-yoga)
Nish-chaya-en yok-tavya = to be known certainly
Chitta-se = from the mind
= certainly
Yoga = meditation-yoga
= is to be done.

Yoga-sañña-jitam = the definition of 'yoga' is -
'That which is known as "yoga" is the conjunction of sorrows and separation from it.'

If we consider the relationship with the world as a conjunction, and not as a separation, this is what is called 'dukh-sam-yog' (conjunction of sorrows). This is not 'yoga'. If this conjunction of sorrows were 'yoga', then there would never be a separation from it. But when one attains knowledge, this separation occurs. This proves that the conjunction of sorrows is only what we consider it to be, what we have created, and not natural.

Even if we consider the conjunction with great determination and for a long time, it will never be a conjunction. Therefore, we can certainly separate from this conjured-up conjunction of sorrows. By separating from this conjured-up conjunction of sorrows (the world-body), we attain the natural 'yoga' (union with the Self), i.e., the experience of our true nature.

Here, we should understand 'yoga' as the natural union with the Self, and not the conjunction with the world-body.

The separation from the world-body (dukh-sam-yog) is called 'yoga' here, and in another chapter, the definition of 'yoga' is given as 'sam-tvam yoga uchyate' (sameness is called 'yoga'). Here, the description is of the goal (sadhya) of sameness, and there (in another chapter), the description is of the means (sadhana) of sameness. These two are the same in reality, because the means of sameness ultimately leads to the goal of sameness.

Patanjali Maharaja has said that the restraint of the modifications of the mind is 'yoga' - 'yogash chitta-vritti-nirodha' (Yoga Sutras 1.2), and when the modifications of the mind are restrained, the state of being established in the true nature of the seer is described - 'tada drastuh svarupe avasthanam' (1.3). But here, the Lord has said that the state of being established in the true nature of the seer is 'yoga', which is self-evident.

What is the meaning of 'tam' here? In the 18th verse, the characteristics of the yogi are described, and in the 19th verse, the example of the lamp is used to describe the state of the yogi's inner consciousness. The yogi's mind, which is in a state of calmness, is indicated by the word 'yatra' in the beginning of the 20th verse, and when the yogi's state is established in the Supreme, it is indicated by the word 'yatra' at the end of the 20th verse. In the 21st verse, the greatness of the yogi's ultimate happiness is described by the word 'yat' in the beginning, and the yogi's state is indicated by the word 'yatra' at the end. In the 22nd verse, the yogi's benefits are described by the word 'yam' in the beginning, and the yogi's benefits are described by the word 'yasmim' at the end. In this way, from the 20th verse to the 22nd verse, the word 'yat' is used six times to describe the yogi's unique state, and here, the word 'tam' is used to indicate that state, and its greatness is described.

'S nish-chaya-en yok-tavyo yoga-anir-vi-ñña-chetasa' - 'moha' (delusion) 'smriti' (memory) 'labdha' (attained) - is said. Therefore, this yoga is not new.
